name: Temoq
confidence_why: No published description of Temoq phonology exists, and the only stress statements that cover it are family-level generalisations that Aslian words stress the final syllable (Blagden 1906, Diffloth 1976 as cited by Dunn et al. 2011, Benjamin 2012, Matisoff 2003), with Dunn et al. 2011 explicitly leaving Temoq out of their sample.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level generalisation only: in Aslian languages (Temoq included by membership, never by name) the word-final 'major' syllable of the iambic (sesqui)syllabic word carries the stress; there is no Temoq-specific statement in any source I could open.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned for Temoq; Aslian-level sources describe an unstressed 'minor' presyllable before the stressed major syllable (Matisoff 2003: 11; Benjamin 2012: 178).
new_statements.exceptions: Blagden 1906: 773 (same family-level claim, 1906 data): 'As a rule, the accent in all the aboriginal dialects appears to fall on the final syllable. This is most marked, however, in Sakai.. but the tendency is also traceable in Jakun'; he adds that in Semang (Northern Aslian) the accent is weaker and 'in some other dissyllables and polysyllables Semang accents the penultimate'. Dunn et al.'s 'most Aslian languages' hedge concerns CVC shape, not stress. Benjamin 2012: 187 notes Southern Aslian (Mah Meri, Semelai) allow open CV final syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root/final syllable). The quoted sentence is about the Aslian family as a whole, reported second-hand by Benjamin 2012 from Dunn et al. 2011; it is not a description of Temoq and should not be entered as a Temoq statement.
new_statements.identity_note: No Temoq-specific description exists; the quoted statement is an Aslian-family generalisation (Dunn et al. 2011 via Benjamin 2012) and Blagden's 1906 'all the aboriginal dialects' generalisation. In Skeat & Blagden 1906 the Temoq area is represented by Miklucho-Maclay's 'Orang Hutan of Ulu Indau' list (Glottolog alt-name Ulu Indau), grouped in the south-eastern 'Sakai' subgroup with Bera/Serting (Semelai-type) dialects (vol. II pp. 397-398). Matisoff 2003 (p. 11 fn., with Benjamin's note) treats Temoq as a dialect of Semelai (ca. 350 speakers per Laird); Glottolog places it in a Semelai subgroup.

sources.note: Family-level only: Aslian languages have 'typically iambic sesquisyllabic (one-and-a-half-syllable) accentual patterns' (p. 178), 'major (i.e., stressed, word-final) vowel systems' (p. 179), and p. 187 quotes Dunn et al. 2011: 300 that the final syllable 'always receives stress'. Temoq is named only in the population table (pp. 141-142, 154) with Collings 1949 as its sole cited documentation; no Temoq-specific phonology.

sources.note: p. 773 'Accent': data 'very meagre'; 'As a rule, the accent in all the aboriginal dialects appears to fall on the final syllable', most marked in 'Sakai', also traceable in Jakun; Semang weaker, sometimes penultimate or evenly distributed. The Temoq-area list ('Orang Hutan of Ulu Indau', Miklucho-Maclay) is grouped in the south-eastern 'Sakai' subgroup (pp. 397-398); no Temoq-specific accent remark.

sources.citation: Matisoff, James A. 2003. Aslian: Mon-Khmer of the Malay Peninsula. Mon-Khmer Studies 33: 1-58.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Family-level: 'Sesquisyllabic forms consist of a major syllable with fully-stressed vowel, preceded by a minor syllable' (p. 11). Temoq appears only in Benjamin's marginal notes: treated as a Semelai dialect of ca. 350 speakers per Peter Laird (p. 11 fn.), 'Temoq thih' for open-final-syllable discussion (p. 13 fn.), dialect continuum Semaq Beri-Semelai-Temoq with vowel length (p. 16 fn.), Mon-Khmer numerals (p. 53). No Temoq stress statement.
